Reconsidering Columbus Day: Why America Should Choose a Different Path

Introduction

Every October, the United States observes Columbus Day, ostensibly celebrating the man credited with "discovering" the Americas in 1492. However, this federal holiday increasingly represents a troubling contradiction to modern American values of human rights, dignity, and historical truth. The time has come to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with a commemoration that better reflects our nation's aspirations for justice and our complete understanding of history.

The Historical Record: Beyond the Myth

For generations, American schoolchildren learned a sanitized version of Christopher Columbus—a brave explorer who proved the world was round and opened the Americas to civilization. This narrative, however, crumbles under historical scrutiny. Columbus's own journals and contemporary accounts reveal a darker reality that cannot be reconciled with contemporary values or historical accuracy.

Upon arriving in the Caribbean, Columbus immediately viewed the Indigenous Taíno people through the lens of exploitation. In his own words, he wrote to the Spanish monarchs that the natives "ought to make good and skilled servants" and could easily be converted to Christianity "as they appear to have no religion." Within mere days of contact, he was already conceptualizing the enslavement of an entire people.

As governor of Hispaniola, Columbus instituted systems of forced labor that decimated Indigenous populations. The encomienda system he established required Indigenous people to provide gold quotas or face brutal punishments, including the amputation of hands. Contemporary chronicler Bartolomé de las Casas, who witnessed these events firsthand, documented mass suicides among the Taíno people who preferred death to the conditions imposed upon them. Within 60 years of Columbus's arrival, the Taíno population of several million was reduced to near extinction.

The Onset of Genocide

The term genocide—the deliberate killing of a large group of people, especially those of a particular ethnic group or nation—accurately describes the consequences of Columbus's governance and the precedents he established. While disease certainly played a role in Indigenous population decline, Columbus's policies of systematic violence, enslavement, and cultural destruction constitute deliberate actions aimed at eliminating Indigenous peoples.

Under Columbus's rule, Spanish colonizers hunted Indigenous people for sport, murdered infants, and worked entire populations to death in gold mines. These were not unfortunate excesses but systematic policies designed to extract maximum wealth from the land and its people. The demographic catastrophe that followed—with Indigenous populations declining by 90% or more in many areas—represents one of the largest losses of human life in recorded history.

The Slave Trade Pioneer

Columbus didn't merely enslave Indigenous peoples locally; he pioneered the trans-Atlantic slave trade from the Americas. In 1495, he captured 1,500 Arawak people and selected 500 to be shipped to Spain as slaves. Approximately 200 died en route and were thrown overboard. This horrific commerce in human beings established patterns of exploitation that would scar the Americas for centuries to come.

The argument that Columbus should be judged by the standards of his time fails under scrutiny. Even among his contemporaries, Columbus faced criticism for his extreme cruelty. Spanish colonist and later priest Bartolomé de las Casas condemned the atrocities he witnessed, and even the Spanish Crown eventually arrested Columbus for his excessive brutality as governor.

What Federal Holidays Represent

Federal holidays are not merely days off work; they represent national values and collective memory. They tell us who we are as a people and what we aspire to be. By maintaining Columbus Day as a federal holiday, we implicitly endorse a historical narrative that celebrates colonialism while minimizing or ignoring the devastating impact on millions of Indigenous people who were already here.

This is not about applying impossible standards of modern morality to historical figures. Many historical figures were complex individuals who both achieved great things and held views we now reject. The difference with Columbus is that his primary legacy—the colonization of the Americas—is inseparable from genocide, slavery, and exploitation. We cannot celebrate the "discovery" without acknowledging that it directly caused one of humanity's greatest tragedies.

The Path Forward: Indigenous Peoples' Day

Abolishing Columbus Day doesn't mean erasing history or denying the complex process by which the modern Americas came to be. Instead, it means choosing to honor a more complete and truthful narrative. Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day—as numerous cities and states have already done—offers an opportunity to:

  1. Honor the First Americans: Recognize the rich histories, cultures, and contributions of Indigenous peoples who inhabited these lands for thousands of years before European contact.

  2. Acknowledge Historical Truth: Present a more accurate account of American history that doesn't begin in 1492 but encompasses the full scope of human experience on these continents.

  3. Promote Reconciliation: Take a meaningful step toward addressing the historical injustices faced by Indigenous peoples and their ongoing struggles for recognition and rights.

  4. Educate Future Generations: Provide an opportunity to teach young Americans about the diverse Indigenous cultures that continue to enrich our nation.

Addressing Counterarguments

Some argue that abolishing Columbus Day erases Italian-American heritage, as the holiday has been embraced by Italian-American communities. However, Italian-Americans have countless figures worthy of celebration who didn't perpetrate genocide—from scientists like Enrico Fermi to artists like Frank Sinatra to the millions of Italian immigrants who helped build modern America. Italian-American heritage deserves better than association with Columbus's brutal legacy.

Others contend that judging historical figures by modern standards is unfair. Yet this argument creates a false equivalence. We're not demanding perfection from historical figures but drawing a reasonable line at genocide and mass enslavement. Many of Columbus's contemporaries, including Spanish missionaries and scholars, recognized and condemned his cruelty. If anything, we're applying the moral standards that existed in Columbus's own time.

Conclusion

The United States stands at a crossroads in how we choose to remember our past and shape our future. Continuing to honor Columbus with a federal holiday sends a message that we value the conquest and colonization over the lives and cultures of Indigenous peoples. It suggests that we prefer comfortable myths to difficult truths.

Abolishing Columbus Day isn't about erasing history—it's about finally telling the whole truth. It's about recognizing that Indigenous peoples were not "discovered" but rather encountered by Europeans whose arrival brought disease, slavery, and death on an unprecedented scale. It's about acknowledging that the Americas' history didn't begin in 1492 but stretches back thousands of years through rich and diverse Indigenous civilizations.

By replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day, we can take a meaningful step toward historical reconciliation and truth. We can honor the resilience and contributions of Native peoples while honestly confronting the darker chapters of our past. Most importantly, we can demonstrate that America is capable of growth, of admitting past mistakes, and of choosing a more inclusive and accurate narrative for future generations.

The question is not whether Columbus changed history—he undeniably did. The question is whether a nation founded on principles of liberty and justice can continue to celebrate a man whose legacy is antithetical to those very values. The answer should be clear: it's time to abolish Columbus Day and choose a holiday that truly represents the best of American values and the full truth of American history.

Every Taíno over the age of fourteen was forced to deliver a certain quota of gold every three months. Those who failed had their hands chopped off and were left to bleed to death.

This system of forced labor was so horrific and the violence so extreme that it prompted the first major humanitarian debate in European history. Abolishing Columbus Day: Confronting the Mythology of a National Holiday

A Case for Truth, Justice, and Historical Accountability

Every second Monday of October, the United States collectively honors a man whose actual historical record reads like an indictment at a war crimes tribunal. Christopher Columbus — celebrated in patriotic mythology as a brave explorer who "discovered" America — was, by the standards of his own contemporaries and certainly by ours, a brutal colonizer, an enslaver of human beings, and the architect of one of the most devastating genocides in recorded history. The continued celebration of Columbus Day as a federal holiday is not merely a harmless anachronism; it is an act of institutional erasure that privileges a sanitized fairy tale over the lived suffering of millions of Indigenous people, past and present. The holiday should be abolished and, ideally, replaced with Indigenous Peoples' Day — not out of a desire to "cancel" history, but out of a commitment to actually confronting it.

The Historical Record: What Columbus Actually Did

The popular narrative most Americans absorbed in elementary school is breathtakingly simple: Columbus, a visionary Italian navigator, sailed west from Spain in 1492, proved the world was round, and discovered the New World. Nearly every element of this narrative is either misleading or flatly false. Educated Europeans had known the Earth was spherical since antiquity. Columbus did not land on the North American mainland. And the lands he encountered were not, by any reasonable definition, his to "discover" — they were home to complex, thriving civilizations that had existed for millennia.

What Columbus actually did upon arrival in the Caribbean is extensively documented — often in his own words. His journal entries and letters reveal a man immediately preoccupied with gold and subjugation. Upon meeting the Taíno people of Hispaniola, who greeted him with extraordinary generosity and hospitality, Columbus wrote to the Spanish monarchs: "They would make fine servants… With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want." This was not an offhand remark; it was a mission statement.

Columbus initiated the transatlantic slave trade almost immediately. On his first return voyage to Spain, he brought kidnapped Taíno people as living trophies. On subsequent voyages, he organized mass enslavement on an industrial scale. In 1495, Columbus and his men rounded up approximately 1,500 Taíno people, selected the 500 deemed most fit for labor, and shipped them to Spain as slaves. Hundreds died during the crossing. Those who survived were sold in Seville.

For the Indigenous people who remained on Hispaniola, conditions were arguably even worse. Columbus established the encomienda system and the repartimiento, forced labor regimes that required every Taíno person over the age of fourteen to deliver a set quantity of gold dust every three months. Those who failed had their hands cut off and were left to bleed to death — a punishment documented by multiple contemporaneous sources, including Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who witnessed the atrocities firsthand. De las Casas described how the Spanish under Columbus's governance "made bets as to who would slit a man in two, or cut off his head at one blow," how they "tore babies from their mother's breast by their feet, and dashed their heads against the rocks," and how they "made a low, wide gallows on which the hanged victim's feet almost touched the ground, stringing up their victims in lots of thirteen, in memory of Our Redeemer and His twelve Apostles."

The demographic consequences were apocalyptic. When Columbus arrived on Hispaniola in 1492, the Taíno population is estimated to have been between 250,000 and several million, depending on the scholarly estimate. By 1514, only 32,000 Taíno survived. By 1542, a Spanish census recorded fewer than 200. An entire civilization — with its own language, religion, art, agriculture, and political structures — was effectively annihilated within a single human lifetime. While European diseases played a significant role in this demographic collapse, the historical record makes unambiguously clear that systematic murder, forced labor unto death, deliberate starvation, and mass suicide driven by despair were major contributing factors, all directly tied to the colonial regime Columbus established.

It is worth emphasizing that these atrocities were considered extreme even by the standards of Columbus's own era. He was arrested and removed from power by the Spanish Crown in 1500, brought back to Spain in chains, after a royal investigation documented his brutal governance. His own contemporaries found his conduct unconscionable. The notion that we cannot judge Columbus by modern standards is therefore doubly flawed: we can, and his own contemporaries already did.

The Holiday as Institutional Erasure

Defenders of Columbus Day often argue that the holiday celebrates Italian-American heritage, the spirit of exploration, or the broader narrative of the "founding" of the Americas. These arguments, however well-intentioned, rest on a fundamental act of erasure. To celebrate Columbus is to celebrate the beginning of a process that resulted in the deaths of tens of millions of Indigenous people across the Western Hemisphere, the destruction of countless cultures, and the establishment of systems of racial hierarchy and exploitation whose consequences persist to this day.

A federal holiday is not a neutral historical marker. It is, by definition, an endorsement — a declaration by the nation that a person or event is worthy of collective honor and commemoration. When the United States government designates Columbus Day as a federal holiday, it sends a clear message: that the colonization Columbus initiated is something to celebrate. For the estimated 6.8 million Americans who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native, this message is not abstract. It is a recurring institutional reminder that the nation they live in officially honors the man who set in motion the systematic destruction of their ancestors.

The psychological and cultural harm of this message should not be underestimated. Indigenous communities in the United States continue to experience the tangible, measurable consequences of colonization: disproportionate poverty, inadequate healthcare, shortened life expectancy, epidemic rates of suicide among youth, and the ongoing struggle to preserve languages and cultural practices that colonial policies deliberately targeted for elimination. To ask these communities to accept, year after year, a national holiday honoring the man who began this process is not a request for tolerance — it is a demand for complicity in their own erasure.

The "Presentism" Objection and Why It Fails

The most common intellectual defense of Columbus Day is the charge of "presentism" — the argument that it is unfair to judge historical figures by modern moral standards. This objection fails on multiple levels.

First, as previously noted, Columbus was judged harshly by the standards of his own time. The Spanish Crown stripped him of his titles and authority. Bartolomé de las Casas, writing in the same century, condemned the treatment of Indigenous people in terms that remain devastating today. The moral framework necessary to recognize mass enslavement and systematic murder as evil was readily available in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — Columbus and his allies simply chose to disregard it when it applied to people they viewed as subhuman.

Second, the presentism argument fundamentally misunderstands the purpose of abolishing the holiday. Removing Columbus Day from the federal calendar is not an attempt to "erase" Columbus from history. No serious advocate for abolition has suggested removing Columbus from textbooks or pretending the events of 1492 did not occur. The argument is simply that he should not be honored — that the United States should not designate a day of national celebration in his name. There is a vast difference between studying history and celebrating it. Germany teaches the history of the Third Reich extensively in its schools; it does not maintain a federal holiday honoring Adolf Hitler. The distinction between remembering and venerating is not difficult to grasp.

Third, the presentism objection, if taken to its logical conclusion, would render moral judgment impossible across any temporal distance, which would mean we could never reassess which figures deserve public honor. Societies evolve. Our understanding of justice deepens. The decision to stop celebrating a figure whose legacy is primarily one of suffering is not an act of retroactive punishment — it is an act of moral growth.

The Italian-American Heritage Argument

Many Italian Americans feel a genuine and understandable attachment to Columbus Day, which has historically served as a celebration of Italian-American identity and contributions to American society. This attachment has deep roots: the holiday was partly established in response to vicious anti-Italian discrimination and violence, including the lynching of eleven Italian Americans in New Orleans in 1891. Italian Americans' desire for recognition and respect is entirely legitimate.

However, the Italian-American community — one of the most vibrant, accomplished, and culturally rich communities in American life — deserves a far better representative than Christopher Columbus. Italy has produced Galileo, Leonardo da Vinci, Enrico Fermi, Maria Montessori, and countless other figures whose legacies are ones of genuine human achievement rather than human suffering. Italian Americans themselves have enriched every dimension of American life, from science and literature to cuisine, music, labor rights, and public service. To suggest that Italian-American pride can only be sustained through the celebration of a man who enslaved and brutalized Indigenous people is, frankly, an insult to the depth and richness of Italian-American heritage.

Several Italian-American organizations and public figures have recognized this and have actively supported the replacement of Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day. The attachment to Columbus is cultural habit, not cultural necessity. Italian-American identity is far too robust and multifaceted to depend on the veneration of a single, deeply compromised historical figure.

The Movement Toward Indigenous Peoples' Day

The good news is that the tide is already turning. As of 2023, more than 130 cities and over twenty states have formally replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day or adopted it as an additional or alternative observance. These include major cities like Los Angeles, Denver, Phoenix, Seattle, and Washington, D.C., as well as entire states including Minnesota, Vermont, Alaska, Oregon, and New Mexico. This growing movement reflects a broad and increasingly mainstream recognition that the values Columbus actually embodied — conquest, exploitation, and dehumanization — are antithetical to the values the United States claims to uphold.

Indigenous Peoples' Day serves a constructive purpose that Columbus Day never could. Rather than honoring a colonizer, it celebrates the resilience, culture, and contributions of Indigenous peoples — communities that survived centuries of systematic attempts at destruction and continue to enrich American life in profound ways. It creates space for education about the true history of colonization, not to promote guilt, but to promote understanding. It honors the living rather than glorifying the architects of death.

Replacing a holiday that causes documented harm with one that promotes recognition, healing, and truth is not "political correctness." It is moral clarity.

Conclusion: Choosing What We Honor

Nations define themselves by what they choose to celebrate. A country that maintains a federal holiday honoring Christopher Columbus is a country that has decided, at the institutional level, that the colonization of the Americas — with all its attendant horrors — is worthy of annual celebration. This is a choice, and it is the wrong one.

The historical record is unambiguous. Columbus enslaved thousands of human beings. He presided over a regime of forced labor, mutilation, and mass death. He initiated a process of colonization that would ultimately kill tens of millions and destroy countless cultures. He was stripped of his authority by his own government for the severity of his crimes. None of this is contested by serious historians. The only question is whether we, as a nation, wish to continue honoring him for it.

Abolishing Columbus Day does not erase history. It corrects a moral error. It acknowledges that the United States is capable of growth — of looking honestly at its past and choosing, deliberately, to honor what is worthy of honor. The resilience and survival of Indigenous peoples in the face of centuries of attempted annihilation is worthy of honor. The courage of communities that have preserved their languages, traditions, and identities against overwhelming odds is worthy of honor. Christopher Columbus is not.

It is long past time for the United States to stop celebrating the mythology of "discovery" and start reckoning with the reality of colonization. Abolishing Columbus Day is not the end of that reckoning — but it is an essential, overdue beginning.

The Myth We Were Sold

We were taught a fairy tale in school. We were given a neat little rhyme: "In fourteen hundred and ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue." We were told he was a hero, a visionary, a brave explorer who "discovered" a new world.

When Columbus first encountered the Taíno people of the Caribbean, he wrote in his own journal that they were generous, peaceful, and intelligent. He wrote, and I quote: "They would make fine servants. With fifty men we could subjugate them all and make them do whatever we want."

That was not the observation of an explorer. That was the calculation of a conqueror.

And conquer he did.

Within years of his arrival, Columbus and his men had enslaved the Taíno people, forcing them—including children—to mine for gold under threat of mutilation. Those who failed to meet impossible quotas had their hands cut off. Cut off. And they were left to bleed as a warning to others.

Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who witnessed these atrocities firsthand, wrote of Spanish soldiers who would test the sharpness of their blades on Indigenous bodies. He wrote of mass hangings, of people burned alive, of babies torn from their mothers' arms.

Before Columbus arrived, the Taíno population of Hispaniola numbered in the hundreds of thousands—some historians estimate as many as several million. Within sixty years, they were virtually gone. Not reduced. Not diminished. Functionally erased from existence.

This is not ancient history too distant to matter. This is the legacy we celebrate with a federal holiday.

We would never—never—create a national holiday honoring a figure who launched such devastation against any other group of people. The very idea would be obscene. So why do we accept it here?

Because justice doesn't wait for convenience. And the truth doesn't care about tradition.

Thank you.
